name: Migrating for Work Safely
objectives: Given a country you want to work in, find the official government and embassy pages for work visas and legal routes, and tell an official page from an agent's or a stranger's page
Given the name of a recruitment agency, check whether the agency is licensed with your country's labour or migration authority, before you pay anything or hand over documents
Given a job advert or recruiter message, list the warning signs of a fake recruiter or job scam, finding at least 3 of 4 signs in a practice advert
Given a job offer or contract, check that the employer, job, pay, hours, place, costs and return terms are written down, and list every missing or changed item before signing
Given a story about a worker abroad, identify the signs of trafficking or forced labour and name where to get help, naming at least 3 signs and 2 places to get help
Before you leave home, write a migration safety checklist with document copies, contacts and help numbers, that covers every part of the course rubric

chapters.name: Chapter 1: Choosing a safe, legal route

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Legal routes and where to find official information
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find the official pages for working legally in the country you want to go to.
This lesson builds toward: Given a country you want to work in, you will find the official government and embassy pages for work visas and legal routes, and tell an official page from an agent's or a stranger's page.
A legal route means you travel with the right visa or work permit for the job, issued by the government of the country where you will work. Working on a tourist visa, or crossing a border with a smuggler, puts you at high risk: you can be arrested, sent home, or trapped by people who know you are afraid of the police.
Only governments decide visas and work permits. Trusted information comes from the official immigration website of the country you want to work in, its embassy or consulate in your country, and your own country's labour or migration ministry. Many countries of origin also have offices that help migrant workers, for example the Department of Migrant Workers in the Philippines and the eMigrate portal of India's Ministry of External Affairs.
Agents, social media pages, video channels and friends can help you get started, but they are not official. Check every fact they tell you on the government page. This course does not give legal or visa advice; if your case is complex, ask the embassy or a licensed lawyer.
Smuggling and trafficking are different. Smuggling is paying someone to cross a border illegally. Trafficking is when someone recruits or moves a person by force, lies or abuse in order to exploit them. Smugglers can turn into traffickers, which is one more reason to use only legal routes.
Step by step:
- Write down the country and the kind of job.
- Search for that country's official immigration or visa website and its embassy in your country.
- Check the address: governments usually use an official ending such as .gov, .gov.ph or .go.ke; look for the government crest and contact page.
- Find the page about work visas or work permits and note what it says you need.
- Find your own country's labour or migration ministry page for people working abroad.
Words to know:
- Legal route: a way to travel and work that the governments allow, with the right visa or permit.
- Work permit: official permission to do paid work in a country.
- Embassy or consulate: your country's office in another country, or another country's office in yours, that handles visas and helps citizens.
- Smuggling: paying someone to take you across a border illegally.
- Trafficking: recruiting or moving a person by force, lies or abuse in order to exploit them.
Official sources:
- UNODC: Human trafficking and migrant smuggling (Education for Justice)
- Philippines Department of Migrant Workers (DMW)
- India Ministry of External Affairs: eMigrate
Try it now: Pick one country you might want to work in. On a phone or computer, find (1) its official immigration or work visa page and (2) its embassy or consulate in your country. Write both addresses on paper and one thing each page says you need.
You can now find the official government and embassy pages for working in another country and tell them apart from agents' pages.

check.q: Who decides whether you get a work visa for another country?
options: The recruitment agent
The government of that country
A popular video channel about jobs abroad
Your future employer alone
check.why: Only the government of the destination country issues visas and work permits.

check.q: A friend says you can work there on a tourist visa. What do you do?
options: Go, because your friend did it
Pay an agent to arrange it quickly
Check the official immigration page or the embassy first
Ask on social media
check.why: Working on the wrong visa can get you arrested or trapped; the official page tells you what is legal.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Checking that a recruitment agency is licensed
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check an agency's licence on your government's official list.
This lesson builds toward: Given the name of a recruitment agency, you will check whether the agency is licensed with your country's labour or migration authority, before you pay anything or hand over documents.
In many countries, agencies that send workers abroad must hold a licence from the government. The licence means the government knows who they are and can act on complaints. An unlicensed agent has no one checking on them.
Examples: in the Philippines, the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) lets you verify the status of a recruitment agency online. In India, the eMigrate portal lists registered recruiting agents, and the agent should show a valid registration certificate. In Kenya, the National Employment Authority (NEA) keeps the list of registered private employment agencies. In other countries, ask the labour ministry, the public employment service, or an IOM office which list to use.
Check the exact name and licence number. Some fake agents copy the name of a real agency, or use a licence that has expired or been cancelled. Check again close to the date you pay or sign, because licences can be suspended. Also check that the job order or vacancy is approved where your country requires it.
Step by step:
- Ask the agency for its full legal name, address and licence number, in writing.
- Open your government's official list (not a link the agent sends you).
- Search for the name and the licence number and check they match.
- Check the licence is valid today and not suspended or cancelled.
- If the agency is not on the list, stop and report it to the authority.
Words to know:
- Recruitment agency: a business that finds workers for employers, sometimes in other countries.
- Licence: official permission from the government to do a kind of business.
- Job order: an employer's official request for workers, which some countries must approve.
- IOM: the International Organization for Migration, the United Nations agency for migration.
Official sources:
- Philippines DMW: recruitment agencies
- India MEA: FAQ on issues of intending emigrants
- Kenya National Employment Authority
- IOM IRIS: Ethical Recruitment
Try it now: Find your own country's official list of licensed recruitment agencies (or the office that keeps it). Write down the web address. Then look up one agency you have heard of, or any agency on the list, and write its name, licence number and whether the licence is valid.
You can now find your country's official list of licensed agencies and check one agency's name, number and status.

check.q: An agent sends you a link to a page that says the agency is licensed. What is the safest check?
options: Trust the link because it looks official
Ask the agent to send a screenshot
Count the good reviews on social media
Open your government's official list yourself and search the name and number
check.why: Fake agents can make fake pages; going to the official list yourself is the real check.

check.q: The agency name matches the official list but the licence number is different. What does this suggest?
options: Someone may be copying a real agency's name
Nothing; numbers are not important
The agency is extra safe
You should pay faster
check.why: Fake agents copy real names; the name and number must both match a valid licence.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Spotting fake recruiters and job scams
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List the warning signs in a job advert or recruiter message.
This lesson builds toward: Given a job advert or recruiter message, you will list the warning signs of a fake recruiter or job scam, finding at least 3 of 4 signs in a practice advert.
Fair recruitment has one simple rule you can remember: workers should not pay to get a job. The International Labour Organization (ILO) guidelines on fair recruitment say no recruitment fees or related costs should be charged to workers or job seekers. The employer pays. This is called the employer pays principle. Some countries still allow certain fees by law, so if anyone asks you for money, check your country's official rules first.
Common warning signs: you must pay a placement, training, medical or visa fee to the agent before you see a contract; the pay is far higher than normal for the job; the offer comes only by social media or messaging with no company address; they rush you to decide today; they ask you to travel on a tourist visa; they want to keep your passport; or the job, the employer or the country keeps changing.
Other signs: you are told to lie to officials at the airport, to borrow money from the agent, or to keep the offer secret from your family. A real employer can be checked: it has a real address, a website, and a job order or contract you can read before you pay or travel.
Step by step:
- Read the advert or message slowly.
- Circle any request for money, your passport or secrecy.
- Check whether the pay and the job make sense.
- Check the company and the agency on official pages.
- If you see a warning sign, stop and ask the authority or a trusted adviser.
Words to know:
- Recruitment fee: money charged to a worker to get a job or be placed in it.
- Employer pays principle: the rule that the employer, not the worker, pays the costs of recruitment.
- ILO: the International Labour Organization, the United Nations agency for work and workers' rights.
Official sources:
- ILO: General principles and operational guidelines for fair recruitment and definition of recruitment fees and related costs
- IOM IRIS: Ethical Recruitment (employer pays principle)
Try it now: Read this practice advert: Hotel jobs in Dubai! Pay 3 times normal. No experience. Send 500 dollars for visa processing today, only 5 places left. WhatsApp only. Write down every warning sign you find (there are at least four).
You can now list the warning signs of a fake recruiter or job scam in an advert or message.

check.q: A recruiter asks you to pay a placement fee before you see a contract. What is this?
options: Normal for every job abroad
A sign the job is very good
A warning sign; workers should not pay to get a job
A government tax
check.why: The ILO fair recruitment guidelines say workers should not be charged recruitment fees; paying before a contract is a key scam sign.

check.q: Which message has the MOST warning signs?
options: Here is our address and licence number; read the contract first
Pay today, keep this secret, and travel on a tourist visa
Please send your CV for the interview
The employer pays your flight; see the attached contract
check.why: Rushing, secrecy and a tourist visa for a job are all warning signs.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Protecting yourself before and after you go

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Reading the job offer and contract
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Check a job offer for the details it must have in writing.
This lesson builds toward: Given a job offer or contract, you will check that the employer, job, pay, hours, place, costs and return terms are written down, and list every missing or changed item before signing.
A fair job comes with a written offer or contract that you can read, in a language you understand, before you pay anything, sign or travel. Ask for a copy you can keep. If you do not understand a word, ask the agency, the labour office or a trusted person to explain it.
Check that it names: the employer and its address; the job and its main tasks; where you will work; the pay, how often and how it is paid; the hours, days off and overtime; the length of the contract; housing and food, and whether they are taken from your pay; who pays the flight, visa, medical test and recruitment costs; and how you can end the contract and return home.
Contract substitution is a common trick: you sign one contract at home and are given a different, worse one when you arrive. Keep a photo of every page you sign. If the contract you are given abroad is different, do not sign it in a hurry; contact your embassy or labour office.
Step by step:
- Get the full offer or contract in writing and keep a copy.
- Use a checklist: employer, job, place, pay, hours, days off, length, housing, costs, return.
- Mark anything missing or different from what you were told.
- Ask for answers in writing before you sign.
- Photograph every page you sign and keep the photos safe.
Words to know:
- Contract: a written agreement between you and the employer about the job.
- Overtime: work beyond your normal hours, which should be paid.
- Deduction: money taken out of your pay, for example for housing.
- Contract substitution: when the contract you get abroad is different and worse than the one you signed at home.
Official sources:
- ILO: General principles and operational guidelines for fair recruitment
Try it now: Write the ten-item contract checklist from this lesson on paper. Then read a practice offer (make one up, or use a real one with your private numbers covered) and tick each item that is written down. Circle each item that is missing.
You can now check a job offer or contract for the details it must have and list anything missing before you sign.

check.q: When should you read the full contract?
options: After you arrive in the new country
Before you pay, sign or travel
Only if there is a problem
The agent reads it for you
check.why: You need to know the terms before you commit money, sign or leave home.

check.q: At the new job you are given a different contract with lower pay. What is this called?
options: A promotion
A normal update
Contract substitution
A bonus
check.why: Swapping in a worse contract after arrival is called contract substitution, a known abuse.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Knowing the signs of trafficking and forced labour
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name the signs of trafficking and the places to get help.
This lesson builds toward: Given a story about a worker abroad, you will identify the signs of trafficking or forced labour and name where to get help, naming at least 3 signs and 2 places to get help.
The United Nations defines trafficking in three parts: an act (recruiting, moving, holding or receiving a person), a means (force, threats, lies, abuse of power or of someone's weak position) and a purpose (exploitation, such as forced labour or sexual exploitation). For children under 18, no force or lies are needed for it to be trafficking.
Signs to watch for: your passport or ID is taken and kept by the employer or agent; you owe a debt that keeps growing and you cannot leave until you pay it; you are not paid, or paid much less than promised; you cannot leave the workplace or housing freely; you are threatened, or told the police will arrest you; you work very long hours with no days off; you are cut off from family and phone.
Help exists. Contact your country's embassy or consulate, the labour office or police in the country where you are, an IOM office, or a trusted worker organisation. Many countries have hotlines for migrant workers and trafficking victims: look up the official number now and save it. If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call the local emergency number first.
Words to know:
- Forced labour: work a person is made to do by threats or punishment and did not freely agree to.
- Debt bondage: being forced to work to pay off a debt that never seems to end.
- Exploitation: using a person unfairly for someone else's gain.
Official sources:
- UNODC: Human trafficking FAQs
- UNODC Education for Justice: crime of trafficking in persons
- IOM: International Organization for Migration
Try it now: Read this practice story: Amina went abroad to clean houses. On arrival the agent kept her passport to keep it safe. She is told she owes 2,000 dollars for her travel, which grows every month. She works 14 hours a day with no day off and is told the police will arrest her if she leaves. Write down every sign of trafficking or forced labour, and two places Amina could get help.
You can now spot the signs of trafficking and forced labour and name places a worker can get help.

check.q: Your employer abroad says they must keep your passport. What is this?
options: A warning sign of forced labour or trafficking
A normal service to keep it safe
A legal requirement everywhere
A sign of a good employer
check.why: Taking and keeping a worker's passport is a common sign of forced labour and trafficking.

check.q: A worker is in danger right now. What is the first step?
options: Post about it on social media
Wait until the contract ends
Call the local emergency number
Pay the employer the debt
check.why: In immediate danger, the local emergency number comes first; then the embassy and other help.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Your migration safety checklist
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a safety plan with your documents, contacts and help numbers before you go.
This lesson builds toward: Before you leave home, you will write a migration safety checklist with document copies, contacts and help numbers, that covers every part of the course rubric.
Before you leave, make a plan. Keep your own passport and documents with you. Make copies: a paper copy at home with someone you trust, and a photo in a safe place you can open from any phone, such as your own email. Do not post photos of your passport online.
Write down your contacts: a trusted person at home who expects to hear from you on set days; the employer's and the agency's full names, addresses and phone numbers; your country's embassy or consulate in the destination country; and the official hotlines you looked up on government pages. Agree a code word with your trusted person that means I need help.
Keep a simple record of your work: the dates and hours you work and what you are paid. Keep your contract photos. If something goes wrong, these records help the embassy, the labour office or a lawyer help you. Then put all of this, with the checks from earlier lessons, into one checklist: that is your final task.
Step by step:
- List the official pages you used (immigration, embassy, your labour ministry).
- Write the agency's name, licence number and how you checked it.
- List every cost and who pays it.
- Tick the contract checklist.
- Write your warning signs to stop.
- Write your help plan: document copies, trusted contact, check-in days, code word, embassy and hotline numbers you looked up yourself.
Words to know:
- Trusted contact: a person at home who knows your plans and expects to hear from you.
- Check-in: a planned message or call to say you are safe.
- Code word: a word you agree on that secretly means I need help.
Official sources:
- IOM: International Organization for Migration
- Philippines Department of Migrant Workers (example of a migrant worker office)
Try it now: Final task: make your migration safety checklist for one real or practice job abroad. Include the official pages, the agency licence check, costs and who pays, the contract details, your stop signs and your help plan. Use blanks like [passport number] instead of real numbers.
You can now write a migration safety checklist that keeps your documents, contacts and help numbers ready before you go.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Official information Uses only an agent's, a friend's or a social media page. Lists the destination's official immigration page and its embassy in your country. Also lists your own country's labour or migration ministry page and what each page says you need. Agency checked No agency check, or the check used a link from the agent. Agency name and licence number checked on the official list and valid today. Also checked that the job order or vacancy is approved where your country requires it. Costs and warning signs Costs are not listed, or a fee to the worker is accepted without question. Every cost is listed with who pays, and at least four stop signs are written down. Checked the official rules on fees in your country and wrote where you checked. Contract details Fewer than six of the ten contract items are checked. All ten contract items are listed and missing ones are marked. Wrote the questions to ask in writing for each missing item. Help plan No help numbers, or numbers taken from the recruiter. Embassy and at least one official hotline, looked up on official pages, plus the local emergency number. Also names an IOM office or worker organisation near the place of work. Documents and contacts No document copies or trusted contact. Document copies kept at home and in a safe place, a trusted contact and check-in days. Also a code word and a plan to record hours and pay. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Where should your passport be when you work abroad?
options: With the agent
With the employer
With a friend you met on the trip
With you, with copies kept at home
check.why: Keep your own passport; copies with a trusted person help if it is lost or taken.

check.q: Why agree a code word with a trusted person at home?
options: To get a discount on calls
So you can ask for help without others knowing
To unlock your phone
To get a visa faster
check.why: A code word lets you signal danger even if someone is listening.
